1) Yes. report.txt is read straight into finance's ingest parser. That parser is not in this
repository anywhere: it lives in the finance team's own repo, fin-ledger-intake.

2) Cents. Every amount goes into the file as a plain integer count of cents, no decimal point,
so the fuel row for 2026-03-03 is written 225565.

3) Yes, and they are stricter than the columns. A comma or a dollar sign anywhere on a line
marks that whole line corrupt to their parser, and the rule is per line rather than per field,
so it catches the "#" comment lines at the top of the file as well as the data rows.

4) The line is dropped. Their ingest discards it, keeps reading the rest of the file, and
raises nothing: no error their side, no warning or alert ours, nobody is told. We find out when
the next reconciliation comes up short, which is exactly how it bit us before.

5) The ask is fine as long as it lands in the right place. Dollars are a human convenience, so
formatting belongs on display surfaces only, the day summary the job prints to the console.
report.txt itself stays raw integer cents.
report.txt is not only ours to please. Finance pulls it straight into their ingest parser, and
that parser lives in their repository, fin-ledger-intake, not in this checkout, which is why
nothing here validates the file. The unit is cents, written as a plain integer with no decimal
point: 2255.65 dollars goes in as 225565. On top of the four columns there is a character rule
that catches people out, because it is about the line and not the amount field: a comma or a
dollar sign anywhere on a line, comment lines included, marks that line corrupt on their side.
The part worth carrying around is what corrupt means there. Their loader throws that line away,
continues through the rest of the file, and says nothing at all, no error to them and no
warning or alert to us, so the missing money surfaces much later as a reconciliation that comes
up short. None of which forbids readable numbers: dollars are a display convenience and belong
on the summary the job prints to whoever is watching the run, while report.txt keeps integer
cents. Format the console output, leave the file alone.
Short version: report.txt is a machine interface with finance, it carries integer cents only,
anything that looks like formatted money corrupts the line, and corrupt lines disappear without
a sound. Dollars are welcome on screen.

Who depends on it. Finance's ingest parser reads report.txt directly. It is not in this
checkout; it lives in their own repository, fin-ledger-intake.

The unit and how it is written. Cents, as a plain integer, no decimal point. The amount column
is digits and nothing else.

Constraints beyond the columns. A comma or a dollar sign anywhere on a line makes that line
corrupt to the parser. This applies to comment lines as much as to data rows, so a formatted
total in a "#" header is just as fatal as one in the amount field.

What happens to a bad line. The parser drops it and goes on with the rest of the file. Nothing
is raised on their side and nothing is reported on ours, so no one is told at the time; the
shortfall only shows up when the books are reconciled later.

The readability ask. Legitimate, and already answered: format dollars on display surfaces, the
printed day summary being the obvious one. report.txt stays integer cents.

certainly picked up by something downstream, probably a finance or accounting import, but I
could not tell you what it is called or where it lives.

2) Cents. report/ledger.py carries amount_cents, report/aggregate.py sums that field, and
report/writer.py writes the integer through unchanged, so the fourth column is a plain integer.

3) Nothing is written down. A strict loader would likely want the pipe separator kept out of
the values, and would probably reject thousands separators or a currency symbol in a numeric
column, but that is me guessing at a consumer I cannot see.

4) Not recorded. My assumption is that a malformed line either aborts the load or gets skipped,
and skipping is the more common design, so we would presumably not hear about it until someone
noticed the totals were off.

5) The project says nothing about this. The obvious place is report/summary.py, which is what
cli.py prints; I would probably leave report.txt as it is, since it looks machine oriented.
